So I'd like to give a simple explanation of our design to show just what sort of calculations are being run by this chemistry engine.

First we refer to things like fire, water, and ice that don't hold a constant solid form as elements.

Next we call solid objects like trees and rocks, even the player character and weapons, materials.

The chemistry engine uses these things to make its calculations based on three simple rules.

First up is rule one. Elements can change the state of materials.

So the leaves on the tree burn up and disappear.

Next is rule two. Elements are able to change each other's states.

So the fire disappeared when it came in contact with the water.

And finally rule three. Materials cannot influence each other's states.

So you can see neither of them changed.

And that's the chemistry engine in a nutshell. The model is an extremely simple one but allows for the expression of all sorts of events.

All these types of interactions in the game are realized by the chemistry engine.

Wait, are electricity and wind a part of chemistry?

In a textbook the answer is of course no, but in the chemistry engine you bet they are.

Aside from rigid body dynamics, we consider all phenomena that occur in nature to be chemistry.

And so for our purposes, things like wind and electricity are all considered to be elements. Again, treating them this way gives us a simplified method with which to model the world.

Given the right situation, elements can also generate energy and impact the physical world. In this way, all the constituent parts of the world we created are governed by our rules of physics and chemistry.

And with that, we had the game that we had hoped to make, one that used multiplication to increase the things you were able to do.

Earlier, Mr. Fujibayashi posed the question, how can we create a game that uses multiplication to expand gameplay? It turns out our answer to this was to build connections between everything in the world.

This means that everything you see in the game is linked together, so to speak.

And these connections don't simply occur by accident. Instead, they're intentionally designed to have an overall consistency and to feel instinctive.

And of course, they contain all sorts of those clever lies we like to tell. But when we started out, we had no guarantee that this sort of approach would work. So I used 2D graphics to quickly create a prototype as a proof of concept. In the world of Breath of the Wild, this multiplicative gameplay is found in the space between situations and goals. One convention we broke with in making Breath of the Wild was to create a world where fun occurs through multiplication, as opposed to one in which fun elements are simply added together in a sum total. They can make an object float when attached to it. We implemented this functionality not to be used as a solution, but as a way to make the multiplicative gameplay even more plentiful. Because of this, it wasn't a major element, but we actually felt that the ability to stick one object to another had a lot of potential. So, when development began on Tears of the Kingdom, Mr. Fujibayashi, the game's director, produced prototypes like this. These were made in Breath of the Wild's game engine by forcefully sticking objects that appear in the game together. By combining objects, he created something new. By the way, the wheels are actually cogwheels that Mr. Fujibayashi stole from a dungeon. So, we began proper prototyping to stick objects together freely. The potential of sticking objects together that we felt with the Octoballoons and the new value gained by combining objects shown by the prototypes. We felt that this could be a gameplay point for this expanded world. In the end, Ultra Hand and Fuse were born. What was once a simple cooking ingredient can now be attached to an arrow to become a powerful way to defeat enemies. The board on the ground over there can also become a flying carpet. A new game design using this system was born. Even if you aren't sure what to use these things for at first, you will come up with new ways to combine them to make something useful. Sticking two things together produces something new. We used this as a guide when preparing this presentation. Which brings us to physics and sound. By combining two technical fields that aren't usually spoken about together, we thought that we might be able to create an interesting story. Today, I invite the lead programmers from each field to discuss this game from their perspectives. And so, I will pass the baton to the lead physics engineer, Takayama-san. Thank you very much. Thank you, Dota-san. When I first saw the prototype, I was excited that this was going to be a great game. But I also knew this was going to be very, very difficult. I said to myself, are we really doing this? Development is going to be chaos. The more I thought, the more I worried. But unlike, it's sometimes important to have the courage to push forward. As expected, the world fell apart. At this rate, the world will destroy itself before Ganondorf comes back. And so began our battle against the true menace of Hyrule. Hello, everyone. I'm Takahiro Takayama. Since I began at Nintendo, I've worked on many games as a programmer. And now, I develop the in-house physics library and tools. I was the physics programming lead on Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. Thank you for having me today. Before we start, like Breath of the Wild, Tears of the Kingdom uses Havok as the base for the physics engine. And on top of that, we have our in-house physics library, which is a foundation for the physics in Tears of the Kingdom. Please let me switch to Japanese now. With the aim of expanding the world by enhancing the multiplicative gameplay, there were two things we attempted, and I'd like to touch on those. The first was to create an entirely physics-driven world. The second was to create a system where unique interactions occur without any dedicated implementation. I'll start out by explaining why we needed an entirely physics-driven world. During development, when we say physics-driven, what we mean is objects have mass and moment of inertia, and they can be controlled using things like velocity and acceleration. So what would the opposite be? What is a non-physics-driven object? It's what we call kinematic rigid body control. It's forcibly moving a rigid body at a velocity calculated from the animation. The implementation is easy, and the results are also visually easy to understand. So we used it quite a bit in the early stages of development for Tears of the Kingdom. However, rigid bodies controlled by kinematics have infinite mass and can break down a physics-based calculation. As seen in this footage, you normally wouldn't expect the metal object to get caught up like this. Practically speaking, this meant chaos for us. The clash between these non-physics-driven objects and Ultra Hand with its high degree of freedom caused daily problems all over the land of Hyrule. It went something like this. I would hear things like, it broke or it went flying, and I would respond, I know, we'll deal with it later, just focus on getting the gameplay in there and trying it out. We were in search of a solution. The key to that solution was in our experience developing Breath of the Wild. This is the cogwheel from earlier that was not functioning properly due to non-physics-driven controls. We connected the two fixed cogwheels with a constraint to transfer velocity and moved one of them with a motor. Because all calculations are now physics-based, all the issues we were facing were now resolved. From this experience, we realized removing all non-physics-driven objects and making everything physics-driven would lead us to the solution we were looking for. In Tears of the Kingdom, gates were initially implemented as non-physics-driven objects and thus were one of many objects that proved problematic when using Ultra Hand. At the time, we were able to break the physics calculations by putting something under the shutter. This was because the shutter was controlled by kinematics. If the player were to place something underneath the gate, the physics calculation would fall apart because this was a kinematic-controlled gate. So to address this, we made the gate physics-driven. This is now controlled by connecting the ground and the gate with a slider constraint. We then added a motor to power it. This would remove all the breakdown. And this wasn't just limited to objects. Player abilities like recall also needed to be physics-driven. While implementation is faster using a non-physics-driven control for a quick gut check, it can also lead to something like this. In the end, like everything else, we also changed

As a result, regardless of what the player does, we have a world free from self-destruction as seen here.

これまでで本作のような高い自由度のある世界では、すべてが物理で動く必要があるということを説明しました。

アップに至るまで、私はプレイヤーがクルマを作って冒険できる世界を目指していましたが、クルマのプログラムのようなものは実装していません。

あくまでもそれぞれの要素、タイヤ、操縦桿、木の板を実装し、プレイヤーがそれらを組み合わせて自由にクルマを実現できるようになっています。

また、この扉も専用のプログラムは実装していません。タイヤ、石の板、鎖の組み合わせで実現されています。

タイヤが鎖を巻き上げて、タイヤの軸が固定されている扉が開くというメカニズムです。

パドルボートも同様です。タイヤ、木の板に浮力、抵抗などの水のインタラクションが加わることで、この事象が生み出されています。

ここまでは事象について紹介してきましたが、ここからは部品の紹介をしていきます。

タイヤはホイール、モーター、シャフトの3つの合体で構成されていて、シャフトはホイールに直接繋がるのではなく、モーターを支えています。

モーターからのトルクがホイールに伝わり、実際に合体が回転することで地面との摩擦により推進力を得ています。

鎖は物を引っ張ったり、動く力の方向を変えたりするために使われます。

長さに応じて数の異なる複数のカプセル合体をボールソケットコンストレイントで連結するという物理構成になっています。

この作では水の抵抗の表現として速度方向への投影面積を使った抵抗の計算を採用しました。

水の抵抗を表現する簡単な方法では全方向での単純な減衰も考えられますが、イカダやボートはより納得感のある動きになるためには面積に応じた速度の違いが重要でした。

私たちが用意した掛け算の遊びの部品はオブジェクトやゾナウギアに限りません。

ここで紹介した水の抵抗計算は全てのオブジェクトに平等に適用され、これによってパドルボートという事象を実現できています。

特別な実装なしでもそれぞれの事象が実現できる仕組みが良い仕組みだと考えて事象を起こす部品を多く実装しました。

私たちが思いもしなかった組み合わせでプレイヤーたちが冒険している様子をたくさん見ることができてとても嬉しいです。

コログたちも喜んでいますね。

ここまででさらなる掛け算の遊びで広がる世界を目指すために私たちが取り組んだこととして全てが物理で動く世界と専用実装なしで事象が起きる仕組みを紹介しました。

これだけで十分でしょうか。いえ、実はこれらだけではまだまだ不十分です。本当に必要なこととして。

チーム全体で取り組むことが必要でした。チームメンバーの一人一人が実現したい遊びを理解して、そのために何をすべきかを理解して制作を進めました。ここからはチーム内の取り組みについてダイジェストで紹介していきます。

まず全てが物理で動く世界を作るためにアーティストやゲームデザイナーと物理パラメータを正しく設定しました。

木、鉄、石など何でできているかの素材を指定するとそのオブジェクトの密度が決まり質量や完成モーメントが自動的に計算されます。計算に必要な体積はシェイプの形状から自動的に計算されます。

例えばティアーズオブザキングダムの板は現実の板に比べて厚く作られています。ゲームの中での視認性や操作性など様々な理由から決まった形状です。

このような場合はシェイプの厚さ通りに自動計算してしまうと重くなりすぎてしまうのでイメージに合う質量や完成モーメントに補正しました。

祠のギミックは全てが物理で動くため設計が厳密なものが多いです。一つ一つの部品が正しく動いているかをいつでも確認できるように全てのギミックを集めた検証状を作りました。

二場所のような複雑なものもエンジニアとアーティストの間で綿密なコミュニケーションで作られました。車輪の大きさや位置は物理的な挙動から調整されそれに合わせた一番良い見た目をアーティストが作りました。

これはタイヤを乗り物の駆動力以外で使うネタです。

ゲームデザイナーが祠のゲームデザインをする時掛け算の遊びを楽しめるようなネタを作ります。

これは板の向きを変えることが正解になっているネタです。

先ほど説明した水の抵抗計算を速度の投影面積を使うようにしたことで生まれました。

水との直感的なインタラクションを使う私の好きなネタです。

事象を起こす部品としてのタイヤもゲームデザインアートの観点物理のコラボレーションからできています。

組み合わせで作られた車を運転する楽しさを重視していたのでサスペンションが付いた時みんなとても良い手応えを感じました。

アーティストがサスペンションを内蔵したタイヤをデザインしましたが世の中であまり見たことがないものなので大変だったそうです。

シャフトがモーターをサスペンションによって支えていてモーターがホイールに駆動力を与えるという物理構成になっています。

モーターから先が上下左右に動くことでタイヤが設置する時間を増やします。

またレンジリミットとプレーン2つのコンストレイントによって稼働範囲をコントロールしています。

最後に携帯鍋を紹介します。

鍋を自由な場所に置けるようになったので鍋が平らなところに置かれるとは限りません。このままでは煮込み料理がこぼれてしまいます。

煮込み料理がこぼれない対策としてアーティストから伸ばせる足をつけようという提案がありました。

最終的には物理の安定性の観点からポットの底にジョイントを入れることにしました。これで無事に煮込み料理がこぼれなくなって嬉しいです。

さらにとてもありがたいことにこの携帯鍋のジョイントはプレイヤーさんたちの自由な発想により別の使い方でも役に立っています。

チーム全体での取り組みについて紹介しました。Tears of the Kingdomの広大な世界を破綻なく作り切るためにはその実現したい世界をよく理解しているゲームデザイナー、アーティストとの連携が必要でした。

これで物理からの説明を終わります。続いてサウンドの長田さんに代わります。ありがとうございました。

これはサウンドの長田さんに話すことになります。ありがとうございました。

ありがとう高山さん。でも何か忘れていませんか?あなたはサウンドチームを忘れていました。こんにちは、私は長田純也です。私は会社に入社した数年間、サウンドエフェクトを作成するサウンドデザイナーとして参加しました。Breath of the Wildの開発から始めた後、私はインハウスサウンドライブラリとツールを開発しました。今日はここに来てくれて本当にありがとうございます。私は今、日本語に切り替えます。

Thank you, Takayama-san, Hosoda-san. Physics and sound are two different fields, but I think they have some things in common when it comes to how they evolved in this game. First, both steer towards a more rules-based system design to allow for greater player freedom. And these designs added another layer of complexity to interactions that occur within the game. As a result, they each created a system that brings new discoveries not only to players but also us developers. As I explained at the beginning, the concept for multi-collectible gameplay was, rather than creating something fun, create a system that makes fun things happen. With Tears of the Kingdom, we aimed to achieve an even higher level of freedom. As a result, rather than determining each object's movement, the physics team focused on creating a system that makes objects move. And rather than creating every sound you heard in the game, the sound team created a system that makes each sound that way. The fact that they focused on and worked hard to tune this system is fascinating to me. Rather than creating unique interactions, create a system that causes unique interactions to occur. I believe this was the essence of the evolution of physics and sound in Tears of the Kingdom. That's all for our presentation. Thank you for your kind attention. And the interpreters you have heard today are from Nintendo of America. Let's have a big round of applause for them, too. Thank you.

## Procedural Grass in 'Ghost of Tsushima'
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ibe1JBF5i5Y

My name is Eric Wolleb, and I'm a graphics programmer at Sucker Punch Productions. This talk is about the procedural grass systems we use in Ghost of Tsushima to achieve our art direction goals. A quick note, barring some unforeseen circumstance, I'll be available in the live Q&A chat for this video when it's presented, so feel free to put any questions you have during the talk there, and we'll answer them as soon as I am able. Ghost of Tsushima is set on the island of Tsushima off the coast of ancient Japan, and from early on, one of the primary goals was to portray the natural beauty of the island. This meant a lot of foliage, giant forests of gently swaying trees, endless rolling hills of grass, and everything in between. Art direction also decided to lean into a painted feel, where instead of having fields of many intermingled types of flowers, shrubs, and ferns, for instance, we opted to have large swaths of a single type of flower, as if painted there by giant brush stroke. Very, very early on, we experimented with traditional grass cards. These ended up not being desirable for our goals for a couple of reasons. First, wind was something we really wanted to push on, and having our animation tied to the entire grass card was very limiting. Second, overdraw was problematic for the density of foliage we were looking to have in our world. Around this time, we found an excellent blog post by Outterra called Procedural Grass Rendering that inspired a lot of our approach. I'll have a link to their blog post at the end of the talk, and I definitely recommend you check it out. So here's what we came up with. This scene considers just over one million blades of grass and renders about 83,000 of them, each individually animating with the wind and taking about two and a half milliseconds end to end. The grass is highly artist-configurable. We use the same grass system for our giant fields of pampas grass, our burnt-out fields, and our huge fields of flowers. The grass interacts with our wind system to help give the player a sense of direction to support our guiding wind mechanic, where the direction of the wind shows the player where to go. The grass reacts to the player and enemies moving through it too. So here's how I'm hoping to organize this talk. We'll talk first about what our compute shaders produce, then how that information gets passed around. Then we'll go into our vertex shaders and how they handle things, followed by how we determine our material data in our pixel shaders. The last section is a bit of a grab bag of things that help pull the whole system together in an actual production engine. So let's get started. The first step for us is chopping the world up into tiles. These tiles contain a suite of textures for things like the height of the terrain, the material to render the terrain as, and for our purposes here, what type of grass to put at that location and how tall it should be. Those tiles are further subdivided into the tiles we actually render. They sample from subsections of the textures in their parent tiles. The textures are 512 by 512, which ends up meaning we have one texel every 39 centimeters or so. For each render tile, we run one compute shader. Each lane in the compute shader gets a position on a grid within the tile and adds a random offset to pick our blade's position. Once we know where it is, we do distance culling and frustum culling. After that, we sample from our previously mentioned textures to determine what types of grass it is and how tall it should be. Lanes that either have the null grass type or have a height of zero are dropped. Now that we're fairly certain we have a grass blade, we do occlusion culling. Late in the project, we found this to be a small perf win in the majority of shots. Each grass blade has a specific type, which determines what artist-authored parameters it uses. Each tile has a 512 by 512 texture that maps each tile position to a grass type, stored as an 8-bit index into an array of grass parameters. You can fairly clearly see the texels of the texture that control the grass type. So instead, we do a gather, then we randomly choose one of the grass types, weighted by our position relative to the center of the four texels. This gives us a smoother dither transition than if we just did a point sample, which is important for making it less obvious that we're driving our grass type from a low-resolution texture. Now, for each lane that's still active, we fill in 16 floats of per blade instance data. Three floats for position and two for the facing direction of the blade. This 2D facing vector determines the direction the blade of grass is pointing. We put the strength of the wind at the blade's position, which drives animation. We place a per blade position-based hash that drives various things on the blade, including animation. The type of grass it is, which determines which set of artist-author parameters to use. Clumping information, which I'll go into more detail on in a second here. And lastly, various parameters for controlling the shape of the blade. These parameters are influenced by a per blade hash, what clump the blade belongs to, the wind, the slope of the underlying terrain, things moving through the grass and pushing it out of the way, the position of the camera, and more. The way the blades interact with those things are all driven by artist-author parameters and are different for each type of grass. I want to draw attention to the clump values I mentioned in the previous slide. Before we added our clumping code, all our fields looked mostly like grass you'd want to golf on. You could increase the randomness per blade to make it look messier, but it didn't look more like a natural field. It just looked random. Real fields vary. Maybe this area is in shadow in the morning and the grass grows less. Maybe this area has a bit more nitrogen in the soil and the grass grows taller. To try and emulate this, we decided to organize the grass into clumps and use which clump the blade belongs to to affect the other parameters. With this shared clump and our distance to it, we can influence the various grass parameters. We can adjust the height. We can have the clump all point in the same direction. So here's an overview of what our shader flow looks like overall. Our first compute shader fills in our instance data and accumulates our blade count. It's also worth mentioning that the low LOD tiles are twice the size of the high LOD tiles but have the same number of grass blades. This means their grass blades are spread out twice as far. Though we do this in some rare cases, we generally rely on an imposter system that uses the underlying terrain. Effectively, we raise the verts of the terrain to match the height of the grass at that location, then offset the depth we write out to the shadow map in a dithered pattern. When we combine this with our shadow filtering, we end up with a result that roughly matches the shadow density of the grass. It's not without its issues though. The discrete nature of the proxy mesh can end up with hard edges that are difficult to resolve. But in the majority of scenes in the game, the results were good and the perf was great. For more fine detail, we relied on screen space shadows to make up the difference. Screen space shadows can't understand the thickness of objects, but our grass is super thin anyway. They don't account for off-screen geometry, but again, with our grass being small, nothing off-screen is going to have a huge impact on what's on screen anyway. So between our imposter geometry and the screen space shadows, we end up with a decent quality shadows that don't blow our perf budget. And here's the in-game result. Moving forward, there's a few improvements to the system that I'd like to make. First, at many times during production, an artist will be placing an asset that they wanted grass on, but we were strictly limited to grass on terrain. Assets have an option to sample the terrain materials when intersecting the ground and blend their material to the terrain's material to have smooth transitions from the height map controlled terrain to artist-authored assets. But since the grass couldn't be placed on those assets, there was often an awkward edge or worse, grass poking out from underneath the asset. In the future, I think it would be worthwhile to have artist-authored geometry flagged as a grass surface that we can procedurally grow blades from. Then the transition between assets and the terrain could be truly seamless. Second, the cubic bezier vertices we produce now are quite flexible and fast, but there are a lot of other types of dense foliage that we could procedurally place. Ferns, ginkgo leaves, or even small rocks could have a very similar vertex count to our current grass, but would be more difficult to procedurally generate. Artist-driven asset support, especially when combined with being able to grow it on arbitrary surfaces, could be very powerful. Maybe we could grow fur cards for high-detailed animals? I'm not sure, but it's something I want to experiment with in the future. Third, because each rendered tile is twice the size of the previous tile, by the time we've switched to the next tile size up, we've dropped three out of every four grass blades. Each tile has the same number of grass blades, which is nice and simple. However, this means that we're tied to lotting out three-fourths of our grass blades at a distance that isn't very easy to change. In the future, we want to disassociate the lotting out from the size of a tile more, so we can push our grass distance out more easily. So, that's how we rendered huge fields of grass within our frame budget and met our art direction goals. We used compute shaders to generate per grass blade instance data that was highly artist-configurable, then used indirect draw calls to get almost 100,000 bezier curves on screen. We supplemented these simple grass blades with procedurally placed artist assets, and used very simple imposters for shadows and fire lines. Although there's still improvements to be made, we're happy with the results we managed to achieve. If you have any questions about what we did or how we did it, feel free to reach out to me on Twitter. I'd love to answer any questions you have. I also want to thank a bunch of people who worked on the grass in Ghost of Tsushima with me. Jasmine Petri for doing all the hard work of the initial prototype and then letting me just make things wiggle for a couple of years. Bill Rockenbeck for helping me fix countless floating point precision issues. Adrian Bentley for letting me break down his office door and berate him with questions. Matt Polman for making the whole thing actually usable for artists. Tom Lowe for all his awesome shadow work. Dave Elder for his great offline terrain AO baking. And Joanna Wang for endlessly tweaking the two score parameters it took to make a rat's nest of vertices look like actual grass. And as a last note, I'd like to point out that we're hiring. We have graphics and gameplay programmer positions we're looking to pick people up for. So if you're interested by what we're working on, please reach out. Thank you so much for watching my talk, and I hope you have a good day. And here's the Altera blog post I promised earlier. You should definitely check it out.

So what this would do is as the game kind of more and more people died and the player base shrunk it would accelerate the game towards a conclusion, that was the idea.

So I kicked off the game, this is what it looked like, it was set up in a room, in a meeting room that happened to have glass walls and I just sticky taped the rules up on the board, told everyone how it worked and I left and went to my desk.

So today we're going to be talking about a series of first steps. Specifically we're going to be looking at strategies for sort of capturing your initial design and coming up with something that you can take back to your team and turn into a great piece of content. Specifically, the first thing you want to look at is what's your primary constraint, right? Another thing that you can do is look at what are the things that every level is going to have in this game, right? What are the basic building blocks of your game that appear in 80% of all of your levels? And you've got this, you're like, well, these are the things that have to be there, right? So if I don't know other things, I can at least start figuring out where I'm going to put my suit store or my upgrade bench or my kiosk, right? Well, step one for building something is to capture the intent or capture your design, right? And what do I mean by this? I think that there are three main components to delivering a design if we're talking about making, like, a single-player level. You've got a concept, which is just this high-level sort of X-statement thing, or your dominant feature, or whatever it's going to be. You've got a walkthrough, which is a description of what you want to build. And it doesn't have to literally be a walkthrough if you're making a multiplayer map or something, but it's a plan of, well, what's the setting of the map? What are the different sort of points going to be? How is everything going to work together? And what's the content going to really entail? And we'll go through each one of these sort of individually. And finally, there's a block world. All of this is the design, and that's the deliverable that we're trying to get to at the end of this. And I said that sometimes you look at a level and you want to be able to say, well, this is the underwater level, or this is the nighttime stealth level, or this is the at-sea level. Just to sell this idea that there's kind of like this latent evil and you're showing up and kind of like kicking it back to life. While this is a common approach, we

to include relevant objects.

このようにコントロールされたカメラでは、必要なものが画面内に自然に映るように設計されるので、プレイヤーにとって遊びやすいゲーム体験を保証できます。

With this sort of controlled camera, we can design the game so that relevant objects naturally appear within the field of view, guaranteeing a smooth and comfortable gameplay experience.

このカメラだからこそ解決できた問題もあります。ホバリングの問題です。

There were other issues that can also be resolved thanks to this kind of camera setup. One of these was the issue of hovering.

この問題について話す前に、ホバリングとは何かを紹介します。ホバリングとは、どこでも好きな時に空を飛べるカービィの技です。

Before we talk about this issue, let me first explain what hovering is. As you can probably guess, hover is an ability that enables Kirby to fly wherever the player wants.

この技を3D空間で行います。開発者にとってこんな恐ろしい技はありませんよね。

This ability is used in 3D space. As a developer, can you think of a more terrifying ability?

ホバリングで自由に飛ぶことができると、どこまでも行ってみたくなります。しかしコースクリア型のゲームでは行ける範囲に制限があります。

If you allow the player to fly around freely by hovering, they'll want to keep going and going. But in a game based on completing each level, there are restrictions on how far you can go.

行ってみないとわからないではスムーズなゲーム体験が崩れ、ストレスになります。この問題に対しても指定カメラを使い、行けない匂いを出すことで解決しました。

Not being able to tell whether you can get somewhere until you try ruins the smooth gameplay experience and can stress out the player. To resolve this issue, we again used the set camera to hint to the player where they can't go.

端まで行かなくても、そっちには何もないことがなんとなく感じれるようになって納得感が出ました。

Even if you don't go all the way to the edge, you can get the idea that there isn't anything there.

このカメラの仕組みは、まずコースを覆うようにカメラだけが当たる壁を設置します。この配置は主に自動で行いました。

The mechanism behind this camera setting is to first create walls surrounding the course that only the camera can hit. This placement was mainly done automatically.

次にカメラの中視点から画面に映したい範囲、放射状へ判定を伸ばします。カービィより先にこの判定が当たることでカメラの中視点を滑らかにずらし、滑らかに動く動きを実現しています。

Next, we sent radial detection lines out from the focal point of the camera within the area we want to show. By having this detection occur ahead of where Kirby is, we can smoothly move the camera focus.

さらに指定カメラだからこそできたアート表現もあります。

In addition, many artistic expressions became possible precisely because of this set camera.

背景をメインに映し大胆にレイアウトしたカメラは、新しいカービィの世界を表現するのに役立ちました。

With the backdrop as the main focus, this bold camera angle serves the purpose of highlighting a new dimension in the world of Kirby.

誰でも遊べる3Dアクションを目指してやったことは以上になります。

That wraps up this section on what we did to achieve a 3D action game anyone can play.

シリーズの転換期に生まれた星のカービィWii、そのリメイク作品になります。

Kirby's Return to Dream Land, released for the Wii, was born at a turning point in the series, and this is a remake of that title.

ベースとなる星のカービィWiiは、かつてゲームキューブの頃から3作もの実験開発を続けました。

Leading up to the original Wii game, Kirby's Return to Dream Land, there were three experimental titles that were created, starting from the GameCube days.

そして4作目にしてようやく世にお届けできた、実に11年ぶりの末置きで遊べる本編カービィとなります。

It was the fourth iteration that finally saw the light of day. This was the first mainline Kirby title for a console in 11 years.

その11年の間、絶え間なく実験開発は続けました。一定のクオリティに達さなければ世に出さないという決意から、我々は長く海の苦しみを味わいました。

During those 11 years, we continued to iterate on experimentation and development. Because we were determined to not release a title until a certain level of quality was met, we went through a long period of many growing pains.

そしてついに全てのスタッフの努力が実り、星のカービィWiiは完成します。シリーズの歴史を語る上でも欠かせないタイトルとなりました。

And finally, the efforts of the entire staff bore fruit, and Kirby's Return to Dream Land was complete. It became a key title in the history of the series.

ではこれより、その歴史の中で積み重ねられてきた2Dカービィにおける創意工夫について、星のカービィWiiデラックスを事例にお話しさせていただきます。

Now, I'd like to discuss some of the creative ingenuity that we have been able to accumulate through the history of 2D Kirby titles, using Kirby's Return to Dream Land Deluxe as an example.

星のカービィは初心者から上級者まで、間口が広く奥深いゲームを目指しています。

Kirby aims to be a series that has approachable yet deep gameplay, enjoyable to both beginners and veteran players.

そのために私たちは様々な工夫を積み重ねてきました。その工夫もある考えをもとにしています。

To this end, we have accumulated a variety of inventive methods, and these methods are all based on a certain concept.

それはカービィをヒーローにすることです。

That concept is, make Kirby the hero.

カービィをまるでヒーローのように奮闘し、敵に打ち勝つ存在であってほしく思います。

We want Kirby to be a heroic figure who fights valiantly to defeat his enemies. In order for Kirby, and by extension the player, to become the hero, we feel it is essential to have controls that feel right.

プレイヤーの思い通りに動くことが本当の気持ちよさにつながります。プレイヤーがうまくキーを入力したつもりでも、実際は正しく入力できていないことがあります。

What leads to feeling right is when a character moves exactly the way the player intended. There are times when a player thinks they pressed the button at the right time, but in reality, the input was a bit off. From this sort of fuzzy input, we predict what the player intended Kirby to do and have Kirby behave according to the player's intent. I'd like to share with you a few of the many mechanisms that demonstrate this.

空中でジャンプボタンを押すと、通常はホバリングが発生します。

If you press the jump button while in the air, Kirby would usually begin hovering.

しかし着地する直前にボタンを押したとき、プレイヤーはジャンプするつもりでホバリングしてしまうことがあります。

However, if the button is pressed just before landing, you may get a situation where the player intended to jump but ends up hovering.

そんな状況でもプレイヤーの思いを予測し、キー入力通りのホバリングではなくジャンプに移行するようにしました。

In these situations, we predict the player's intent and make it so Kirby jumps instead of strictly following the button input and hovering.

また、穴を飛び越えようとボタン操作が遅れてしまった場合も、

Even in situations where the player presses the button too late to jump over a pit,

プレイヤーの思いを予測し、空中でもジャンプさせています。

we predict the player's intent and make Kirby jump even in midair.

さらに、カービィがジャンプした際、頭上に発生する攻撃判定についてもプレイヤーの思いを予測し工夫がなされています。

Even the hit detection on Kirby's head during a jump has been adjusted so that it matches the player's intent.

これはダッシュしながらジャンプした時のスロー映像です

アークモードが完成しました。 Our goal with the flow of the game was ease. We made it easy to go back and forth between modes mid-game with the press of a single button. We then carefully considered his abilities, role, and personality. 彼はゲーム中よく話し、どこか守ってあげたくなるけど怪しさも存在する存在です。 He speaks a lot in the game. In this game, we leveraged some of the unique characteristics of his outfit, such as parts of it falling off to denote that he's in trouble. また機械音声ですが、ボイスのあるキャラクターなので口元を隠すことで大量の会話デモを作りやすくします。 And despite his voice being a synthesized one, he is still a voiced character, so we hid his mouth to make it easier to create many conversational scenes. ちなみに彼の声は本作のサウンドクリエイターのもので、実は中身は50代のベテラン作曲家です。 Incidentally, he is voiced by the sound creator of this game, so on the inside, he's a veteran composer in his 50s. カービィ以外の声は割とチームメンバーが担っているものもあります。 A fair amount of voices other than Kirby's are done by other team members. 例えば近年のデデデダイオーのように。 Like, for example, King Dedede. こちらは本作を作るにあたり描いた世界を表す概念図です。 This is a concept diagram that we drew up when we were creating this game. Our goal was to summarize the overall mode through symbolic buildings and make it possible to see all the doors to the many subgames at a glance. シリーズを続ける中で常に新しいものを取り入れていますが、役割と個性から考え、数々のデザイン案からようやくカービィの世界の一員になれるものが生まれます。 As we continue the series, we are always incorporating new things. But when we do, it's not until we consider their roles and characteristics and brainstorm many design proposals that something that will become a part of the world of Kirby is finally born. この他にも本作ではご紹介した間口の広いテーマパークモード以外に、奥深さを感じられるモードも作りました。 In this game, in addition to the approachable amusement park mode that we introduced, we also created a mode where players can really feel the sense of depth that we mentioned before. それがマホロアエピローグです。 That mode is the Magolor Epilogue. マホロアエピローグはクリア後にオープンとなるより歯応えのあるモードです。 The Magolor Epilogue becomes available after completing Story Mode and is a mode that offers a greater challenge. まずはこのモードのゲームシステムを簡単にご紹介します。 I'll start with a brief overview of the game system for this mode. このモードは魔力ポイントを集めてキャラクターを強化していくゲームになります。 In this mode, you collect magic points and use them to enhance your character's abilities. 力を失ったマホロアが復活を目指すという物語にリンクさせることで、冒険の動機と導入への納得感を高めています。しかし、それはあくまで副次的な理由です。 The game system is tied to a story in which Magolor has lost his powers and wants to get them back. ## 'Death Stranding': An AI Postmortem
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yqZE5O8VPAU

Hello, my name is Eric Johnson. I'm an AI programmer at Kojima Productions, and today I want to share with you some of the AI features we built, challenges we faced, and things we learned during the development of Death Stranding. This is primarily a navigation talk. To that end, I want to begin by discussing the game environment and why it was such a challenge for us to work with, game design's goals for NPCs and how they affected our approach to dealing with the environment, how we reflected the complexity of the terrain on the navmesh, the impact this complexity had on navigation, support for different types of dynamic terrain, a quick look at a trick we used to improve position selection in our environments, and a peek into a few of the other AI systems we built for the game. First, I want to give special thanks to Guerrilla for providing us with the Decima engine on which Death Stranding is built, as well as the ongoing support they've given us throughout development. I also want to thank the rest of the NPC team at Kojima Productions, whose work I'll be sharing with you today. Without them, this talk would not be possible. So, as most of you are probably familiar, Death Stranding is a game with a heavy focus on environmental traversal, deciding your route, what equipment to bring, and how to approach the landscape, overcoming environmental obstacles using a variety of tools at your disposal, such as ropes, ladders, and bridges, all in order to ultimately reach your destination. But it's not just these large-scale obstacles you need to worry about. Even flat terrain is difficult to traverse. You can lose your balance and stumble, slip in the mud when it rains, or lose your footing on steep slopes, or get swept away by the current of rivers. Every step has the potential to be hazardous. So, to create an environment where even walking would be a challenge, in the early days of the company, the team went location hunting in Iceland to gather reference material. While they were there, they toured volcanic rock fields, rivers, valleys, and gorges, crevices, caves, and geysers, which they referenced to create environments like these. Take a look. So, these were the types of beautiful but unforgiving landscapes the environment team had created to challenge the player. But if this terrain was meant to be difficult for the player to traverse, this meant it was going to be even harder for the AI. Because while the central challenge is overcoming the environment, it's not the player's only obstacle. There are, of course, enemy encounters, and the ones I want to talk about today are mules, melee enemies that chase after the player and steal their cargo, terrorists, ranged attackers whose target is the player and who can use cover, and catchers, giant BTs who need to be able to navigate around, climb on top of, and even destroy dynamic terrain. During the concept phase, the core gameplay loop revolved around the cat-and-mouse game of mules searching for and stealing the player's cargo as the player attempted to make it through hostile territory to complete their delivery. Because they need to steal packages directly from the player, as much as possible we would need to provide traversal parity. Wherever the player could move, mules would need to be able to follow. Similarly, if cargo was dropped onto the terrain, NPCs would need to be able to reach it to pick it up wherever it lands. Finally, a lot of effort was placed on making the player interact realistically with the terrain to feel grounded. We wanted NPCs to have a similar level of fidelity. Here's where we started. This is our first AI prototype. You can see here the mules are searching the area for cargo. The player can subdue them with a non-lethal takedown. And while still undetected, they are able to escape and make their way towards the cargo destination. A year later, we had added more non-lethal weapons like the bola gun. NPCs could now respond to noise and perform investigation behaviors. Perception had been iterated on, enabling the player to evade the enemy in tall grass. But NPCs now had the ability to ping the player's cargo to track them down. Still, the gameplay loop remained focused on evading and escaping rather than fighting. And here's the final version that we shipped. When the player enters mule territory, their cargo is pinged. A search party is formed and a group of enemies move to the ping location to try and find the cargo that was detected. This gives the player an opportunity to escape while they're searching for the package. If the player successfully evades the enemy long enough, they will re-ping the area and the cat and mouse game begins again. But if the player is spotted, all mules in the encampment will immediately begin chasing the player to steal their cargo, switching gameplay from evasion to escape. This is the core loop the NPC team was responsible for delivering, and one of the major components in doing so was developing reliable navigation over the terrain. So why is this terrain such an issue, and what kinds of problems does it create for the navmesh? To explain, let's start by looking at some navmesh that represents what we were used to seeing in a typical production. Here is a man-made environment with flat level ground, open spaces, clearly defined walls and corridors. There are challenges in navigation over a navmesh like this, positioning, finding cover, flanking, but these are ones that we were generally familiar with and knew how to handle. Likewise, in natural environments, navmesh was often just a continuous sheet with the occasional hole where rocks, trees, and other obstacles have been placed to decorate the terrain. However, because the environment in Death Stranding was designed first as an obstacle for the player, our navmesh now looks like this. Everywhere we looked, there were jagged shapes with sharp turns, thin strips of navmesh, and tiny disconnected navmesh islands covering the landscape. And I think the sheer volume of games made in game a week facilitates that kind of a taste evolution. A huge part of becoming a successful professional artist is learning to take your own work seriously and hold yourself to a professional standard. And I think one of the nicest things about this class is that it offers students a chance to be recognized as peers by the teacher and by the other students, but I think most importantly in their own eyes. The class doesn't work as well without a sense of high occasion when the weekly themes are revealed. So if anybody wants to run a similar class, I would really strongly suggest using a similar ritualization of the theme presentations to give the students that sense of occasion and an extra boost of motivation. And finally, of course, one of the main reasons to run a class like this is the same as the reason to do it in your own creative practice outside of school, which is that by building a very large number of projects, you have a chance to identify and really hone your own creative identity and explore different expressions of that identity. And that's really about it. We have one minute left, so probably not enough time for questions. We do, however, we've linked our syllabi publicly. Mine's annotated and my syllabus also includes Michael and I's weekly extensive theme notes, so please feel free to take a look at those. And Ben and I are both super happy to answer questions, whether that's by email or in person out in the hall after this talk. So that's about it. Yeah, thank you so much for coming.
Thanks very much.

そうした中で、新しい秘密や不思議がいっぱいの2Dマリオを作るという目標でプロジェクトが始まりました。

However, as 2D Mario has been played for many years, at some point all of this has become normal. For that reason, this project began with the goal of creating a 2D Mario game full of new secrets and mysteries.

私自身、初代スーパーマリオブラザーズを思い返してみて、土管に入ると地下のエリアを冒険できたり、ブロックを叩くとツルが伸びて上空のエリアに行けたり、といった要素が秘密や不思議の象徴だったのではないかと考えました。

I think back to the first Super Mario Bros. and the elements that represented secrets and mysteries to me back then. Elements like entering the warp pipe and being able to explore the underground area, or hitting a block, seeing a vine come out, and climbing that vine to an area in the sky.

そこで最新作では、これらの新しいバージョンを生み出そうと考えて、ブロックを叩くと特別なアイテムが出てきて、このアイテムを取ると別のエリアに行けるというものを作ってみました。

Therefore, in the latest game, I thought about creating a new version of these secrets and mysteries, and I tried making something where when you hit a block, a special item comes out, and if you take this item, you can go to another area.

それを手塚に見せたところ、これやと今までと変わってへんやん、別のエリアに行くんではなくて、その場が変化するようにできへんの?と言われました。

When I showed that to Mr. Tezuka, he said, this isn't so different from how it's always been. Can't you make it so instead of going to another area, the environment itself changes?

どうせだったら思いっきり変化させてやろうと思って、土管がくねくね動いたり、パックンフラワーが歌いだしたりと、これまでのスーパーマリオではなかったような思い切った変化を作りました。

So I thought, well, if I'm going to change the environment anyway, I might as well go hard. So I made drastic changes that have never been seen in a Super Mario Bros. title. I made the warp pipes wiggle and the piranha plants break out in song.

土管がくねくね動くの試作はこんな感じでした。

ちなみに私が今胸につけているバッジは私の娘による手作りです。

ハードの進化とともにゲームの制作規模に比例して開発人数の規模も増えています。Sの時代にはなかったチーム運営という仕事が今重要になっています。

As hardware has evolved, the size of development teams has increased in proportion to the scale of game production, and something we didn't focus on during the NES days, which was team management, is now an important job.

たくさんの人が同じ方向を向いて、できるだけ無駄なく制作していく。このことは100%大切なんですが、実はもっと重要なことがあります。

Getting lots of people working in the same direction to develop a game with as little waste as possible is without a doubt an important job. However, there is something even more important.

たくさんの人数で作るということは、たくさんの頭が存在するということ。それぞれの個性や力をいかに制作に反映できるかということです。その目的のためにチーム運営自体を開発するべきであると思います。

Working with many people means we are also working with many abilities and approaches. So, it's about how can we represent each person's individuality and strengths in production, and team management should be developed for this purpose.

我々も常に試行錯誤していますが、毛利からどうやってチーム全体でワンダーを作ってきたかを話してもらいます。

秘密や不思議がいっぱいにするには、ワンダーの種類がたくさん必要です。そこでアイデア会を開催し、ワンダーのアイデアをチーム全員で出し合いました。

Many types of wonder effects are needed to fill a game with secrets and mysteries. We therefore held brainstorming sessions where the whole team shared their ideas for wonder effects.

アイデアを出すのは職種や年次に関係なくチーム全員です。任天堂はチーム全員がゲームデザイナーと考えています。

It was up to everyone on the team to come up with ideas, regardless of job title or seniority. Nintendo believes that everyone on the team is a game designer.

最初は特に条件などは考えずに、閃いたアイデアをどんどん付箋に書いてもらいました。最初からルールがあると自由にアイデアを出せませんからね。

At first, we asked everyone to write any and all ideas on sticky notes without any conditions. After all, if you start with conditions, you stifle creative freedom.

ここで約2000個のアイデアが出ました。

At this stage, we collected around 2000 ideas.

出てきたアイデアをいろいろ見ていく中で、こういうワンダーは良いという条件が少しずつ絞られてきます。

As we looked at the various ideas that came up, we were able to gradually narrow down what criteria made up good wonder effects.

その一つが、ワンダー前とワンダー発動時に関連があるもの。

Among these ideas, the ones we liked had a connection between pre-wonder effect and during wonder effect.

例えば、プレイヤーがワンダーでいきなりバルーンマリオに変身すると唐突すぎて違和感がありますが、最初に風船のような敵を登場させてからワンダーでバルーンマリオに変身すれば違和感がなくなります。

For example, if the player were to suddenly transform into balloon Mario due to a wonder effect, that would feel unnatural. However, by having balloon-esque enemies appear first, then having the player transform into balloon Mario due to a wonder effect, the feeling of unnaturalness is removed.

他には、今までできなかったことができるようになるものだったり、一言で説明できるもの。こういったものが良いワンダーであることがわかってきたので、該当するワンダーを試作していきました。

Other features that we pinned as good wonder effects were having players suddenly be able to do something that they couldn't before, and having effects that could be explained simply in one short phrase. With these figured out, we started to try out different ideas that met these criteria.

試作もチーム全員で行いました。

This testing phase was also conducted by everyone on the team.

各試作はゲームデザイナー、アーティスト、プログラマー、サウンドが一名ずつで構成された小さなチームで作られます。

過去のアーケードゲームからの流れを利用した新しい仕組みだったと思います。このゲームサイクルは過去のアーケードゲームからの流れを利用した新しい仕組みだったと思います。その後、マリオ3の制作ではボードゲームのようなマップシステムを導入してコースをクリアしていくだけでない遊びの要素を追加してみました。それでもコース攻略が分かりやすい一本道というスタイルを大事にしてきましたが、過去と現代では遊ぶ人の好みも変わりました。今ではマリオにとってどんな課題があって、マリオワンダーではどのように考えるようになったのか、毛利から話をしてもらいます。続いて、ゲーム攻略とプレイヤーの自由度について説明します。過去の2Dマリオではワールドマップ上で最低限の分岐は存在しましたが、複数のコースから遊びたいコースを選んだり、クリアできないコースを飛ばして先へ進むような自由度はありませんでした。また、プレイヤー性能もファイヤーマリオ、しっぽマリオ、マントマリオなどの様々なパワーアップ変身がありましたが、このコースはこの変身のようにコースに紐付いていたので、自分の好きな能力を選ぶことはありませんでした。自由度が低いという課題を解決するために、ワールドマップで自由に移動できるエリアを用意し、複数のコースの中から好きなコースを選択して進めるようにしました。自由に移動できるので、コースのサムネイルを見て面白そうなコースからプレイしたり、難易度の低いコースからプレイしたり、お手軽なちょっと一息からプレイしたりを選択できます。苦手なコースを飛ばして先に進むことも可能です。キーワードアイテムのワンダーシードを一定数集めると先に進めるという構造は最初に決めました。バッジはプレイヤーに好きな能力を選んで付けられるシステムです。これら複数の対応で自由度が低いという課題を解決しました。遊びを考えるときにどんなふうに遊んでほしいかというイメージがあったほうがいいと思います。例えば家族でマリオを遊んだときにどんな姿を想像するか。ネットワーク経由で知らない誰かと遊ぶときにどんな姿を想像するか。毛利さんはどんな遊び方を想像しましたか。家族でお裾分けで遊ぶ場合は予想外のワンダーが発生してみんなが笑顔になることを想像していました。あとオンラインで知らない誰かと遊ぶときは自然とありがとうと言いたくなるような遊びを目指していました。それは素敵ですね。スーパーマリオでのオンラインの遊びはどうあるべきか。プログラマーでありゲームデザイナーの毛利さんの考えを聞いてみたいと思います。続いて新しいオンラインについて説明します。2Dマリオを進化させるため今回はオンラインで遊んで楽しいマリオにするという構想が最初からありました。ただオンラインで世界中の人と遊ぶことはすごく楽しい反面いくつか課題もあります。例えば対戦ゲームは初心者は負け続けてやめてしまう。協力ゲームは苦手な人が足を引っ張ってしまうかもしれない。それからマナーの悪い人がいてトラブルになってしまうことも考えられます。こういった課題は任天堂の社内でも以前から言われていました。実際岩田も例えば親が自分の子供に安心してオンラインの遊びを渡せるにはどうしたらいいんだろうか。ハラスメントのない世界はどうやったらできるだろうみたいなことを私たちはずっと議論していたんですと言っていました。この課題を解決する方法はいろいろありますがマリオワンダーでは他のプレイヤーが自分に直接干渉することなくミスをした時に助けてくれたりアイテムを分けてくれたり自分にとって良い行動しか起こさないようにしました。その動画はこちらです。他のプレイヤーにブロックを壊されたり敵を倒されたりしないことを明確にするため他のプレイヤーを半透明のライブゴーストという形で実装しました。ですがライブゴーストには課題があります。それは同じコースをプレイしている人が常に近くにいるとは限らないということです。この課題を解決するために自分の分身としてパネルを設置できるようにしました。このパネルですが自分が置いたパネルでは自分自身は復活できない仕様にしました。また周りの人に隠し要素を伝えるために置くこともできます。ゲーム制作もオンラインの遊びも多くの人が関わります。人と人が関わるとき大事なのは自分のためではなく周りの人のために行動することではないでしょうか。周りの人が困っていたら助ける。マリオワンダーのオンラインの遊びも自分のためではなく周りの人のために行動するそういう優しい世界を作り上げたいと考えました。親が自分の子供に安心してオンラインの遊びを渡せるにはどうしたらいいんだろうか。ハラスメントのない世界はどうやったらできるだろうといったことを私たちはずっと議論していたんですが今回のオンラインの遊びはその答えの一つになったと思います。毛利さんありがとうございました。開発中にマリオにとってのオンラインプレイは緩いつながりというテーマにしていました。マリオゲームにとって理想とするオンラインを使った遊びには一つの答えが出せたと思います。さて任天堂には何かゲーム作りの秘密があるのではと思う方もいるかもしれません。実はゲーム作りには決まった方法があるわけじゃないです。プロジェクトごとに何を大事にして作るかは違うでしょうし本当に自由です。マリオワンダーでは毛利が話したような作り方をしました。様々なワンダーの要素や試作、遊びの種を作りながらそれらの成果物を生かす最善のまとめ方を考えるということをしました。制作が始まった時には決めてないけども作りながらある時期になって食材が揃ってきたのでどんな料理にしようかなという感じです。走りながら作るということだと思いますが正直不安を抱えながら走ってきたと思います。そんな中で試行錯誤しながらユニークなキャラクターも生まれました。ジャジャーンマリオワンダーにはおしゃべりフラワーという変わったキャラクターが登場します。唯一フルボイスで話すキャラクターです。ゲームの中には臨場感を増すために様々なエフェクト効果やグラフィックサウンドを使います。過去マリオゲームである範囲のコインを全て取った時に拍手を鳴らすという仕様を入れたことがあります。ゴールした時のファンファーレはゲーム中のプレイを褒めてほしいから用意しましたがもっと頻繁に軽い達成感があるとよりゲームに没入できると考えました。これを発展させたものがおしゃべりフラワーです。このキャラクターの一番の目的は応援や共感によってプレイヤーの気持ちを高めて遊びの手応えを大きくすることです。つまりエフェクトのように遊びを助けるために作りました。先ほど話をしたプレイヤーの気持ちを盛り上げて遊びをリアルにするということに貢献しているのではないかと思います。まだまだ話をしたいことはいっぱいあるのですが2Dとその未来の話をするべきです。森さんありがとうございました。ゲーム作りには様々な方法があると話しましたが我々のゲーム作りで最初に深く考えるのはゲームの核になる部分です

2D、3Dで違うということを言いたいのではないです。どちらも同じくらい時間がかかりますが、2Dマリオの場合は、例えばコースの制作に終盤まで調整ができたり、そこに新しい提案を入れやすいと言えます。モーリが言うように、タイトルが持つ課題に向き合いながら、今後様々な新しい技術が生まれて、歴史ある2Dの表現と融合されて、遊び自体が変化していくでしょう。今日は2Dゲーム開発について少しは興味を持っていただけたでしょうか。モーリからも2Dゲームは進化すると伝えましたが、その未来は私が一番ワクワクしているかもしれません。ここにいる皆さんの中からも新しい2Dゲームが作られていったり、もちろん我々もその時代ごとに新しい遊びを作り続けたいです。そして最後に一つ言わせてください。遊びを考えるのは超楽しいです。マリオワンダーの開発に関わった全ての人と、また今日のセッションを全力でサポートしてくれた全ての人たちに感謝します。そして皆さん最後まで聞いてくださって本当にありがとうございました。ありがとうございました。
